overview:
South of Casablanca, the Atlantic coast hides two places most visitors never see. El Jadida was the Portuguese fortress of Mazagan for more than 250 years, and its star-shaped walls, sea gate and vaulted underground cistern are listed by UNESCO. An hour further down the coast, Oualidia is a calm lagoon sheltered from the ocean by a line of rocks, known across Morocco for its oysters. This private day trip puts the two together: history in the morning, seafood and the sea in the afternoon, with your own driver and no group to wait for.

The highlight of El Jadida is the Portuguese Cistern. Built around 1514 as a store or armoury and later turned into a water reservoir, it is a vaulted hall of stone columns where a thin layer of water mirrors the arches and a single shaft of light falls from an opening in the roof. Orson Welles filmed scenes of his Othello here. Around it, the old walled town is still lived in: a Portuguese church, a former synagogue, quiet lanes and ramparts you can walk on with the ocean on one side and the port on the other.

Oualidia is a different world: a small village, fishing boats on a turquoise lagoon, oyster beds that have been farmed since the 1950s, and on the hill the ruins of a kasbah built in the 1630s by the Saadian sultan El Oualid, who gave the town its name. You eat oysters and grilled fish at a table by the water, then choose between the beach, a short boat ride around the lagoon, or simply a walk along the shore.

AT A GLANCE
• Duration: about 9.5 hours
• Start and finish: your hotel or riad in Casablanca (pick-up from the airport or Mohammed VI station on request)
• Distance: about 175 km each way, mostly on motorway and a coastal road
• Driving time: about 1 h 15 min to El Jadida, 1 h to Oualidia, 2 h back
• Type: private day trip with an English- or French-speaking driver
• Walking: about 3 km, flat apart from the steps up to the ramparts
• Activity level: easy

WHAT YOU SEE
• The Portuguese Cistern: the vaulted 16th-century hall, its columns reflected in water.
• The Portuguese City of Mazagan (UNESCO, 2004): the sea gate, the Church of the Assumption, the old Jewish quarter and the ramparts with their four bastions.
• Optional photo stop at Azemmour, whose white medina rises above the Oum Er-Rbia river.
• Oualidia lagoon: oyster farms, fishing boats, a sheltered beach.
• The ruined kasbah of Sultan El Oualid and the ruins of the 1940s royal summer palace on the shore.

WHY THIS TRIP WORKS
Most day trips from Casablanca stop at El Jadida and turn back. Continuing to Oualidia adds the best part of the coast: a lunch of oysters a few metres from where they are farmed and an afternoon by calm water. With a private driver you choose how long to stay in each place, and there is no shopping stop.

WHO WILL ENJOY IT
Seafood lovers, couples, families with children (the lagoon is calm for paddling), photographers, and travellers with a free day in Casablanca who want to see something beyond the city.

WHO MIGHT PREFER ANOTHER TOUR
For history in the capital, take the [Rabat day trip](/en-US/morocco/casablanca/tours/rabat-day-trip-from-casablanca-hassan-tower-udayas-kasbah-chellah/da6c1755500285a3c79985ed). To travel down the whole coast and sleep by the sea, see the [5-day Casablanca to Marrakech coastal tour](/en-US/morocco/casablanca/tours/5-day-casablanca-to-marrakech-via-the-atlantic-coast-el-jadida-oualidia-essaouira/1952d9f9e66a9619a2cdcfd7).

PRACTICAL INFORMATION
Bring swimwear and a towel in summer, a windproof layer all year (the coast is breezy even when it is sunny) and cash in dirhams for the cistern, lunch and a boat ride. Lunch for one person with oysters and grilled fish usually costs 150–300 MAD depending on what you order. The cistern sometimes closes for restoration; if it does, your driver spends the extra time on the ramparts and in the old town.
descriptions:
What to expect: a relaxed private day on the Atlantic coast – a UNESCO Portuguese fortress in the morning, oysters and a calm lagoon in the afternoon.

Your driver picks you up in Casablanca and takes the coastal motorway south. After about an hour and a quarter you reach El Jadida, a lively beach town built around one of the best-preserved European fortresses in Africa. The Portuguese founded Mazagan in 1514 and held it until 1769, longer than any of their other Moroccan strongholds; when they finally left they blew up the main gate, and the town stood half empty until Sultan Moulay Abderrahmane resettled it in the 1820s and renamed it El Jadida, "the new one".

You walk in through the main gate and go first to the Portuguese Cistern. Steps lead down into a cool, almost silent hall of 25 stone columns under brick vaults; a few centimetres of water cover the floor and reflect the arches, lit by one round opening in the ceiling. It is one of the most photographed interiors in Morocco and was used by Orson Welles in Othello. From there the lanes of the old town lead past the Church of the Assumption, the old Jewish quarter and its former synagogue, to the Porta do Mar, the sea gate where ships once unloaded directly inside the walls. Climb onto the ramparts and walk between the bastions for views of the ocean, the fishing port and the town.

On request your driver can make a short stop at Azemmour on the way, for the view of its white medina above the Oum Er-Rbia river.

The road then follows the coast south past farmland, dunes and small fishing beaches to Oualidia. The lagoon is about 7 km long, separated from the open ocean by a natural rock barrier, which keeps the water calm and clear. Oysters have been farmed here since the 1950s, and the restaurants along the shore serve them a few hours out of the water, along with grilled fish, prawns, calamari and, in season, sea urchins. After lunch you can swim or paddle on the sheltered beach, take a fisherman's boat around the lagoon to see the oyster beds and the birds on the sandbanks, or walk up towards the ruined kasbah of Sultan El Oualid for the view. In the late afternoon you drive back to Casablanca.

SCHEDULE (times are estimates)
08:30 – Pick-up at your hotel or riad in Casablanca.
09:45 – Arrival in El Jadida; Portuguese Cistern (about 30 min).
10:15 – Old town, Porta do Mar and the ramparts (about 1 hour).
11:30 – Coffee break or free time by the beach in El Jadida (about 15 min).
11:45 – Drive along the coast to Oualidia (about 1 hour).
13:00 – Seafood lunch by the lagoon (about 1.5 hours, not included).
14:30 – Free time: beach, boat ride on the lagoon or walk to the kasbah viewpoint (about 2 hours).
16:30 – Depart Oualidia.
18:30 – Drop-off in Casablanca, depending on traffic.

GOOD TO KNOW
• The cistern has a small entrance fee and is occasionally closed for restoration work.
• Boat rides are arranged directly with local boatmen; about 150–200 MAD per boat for an hour is typical. Your driver can help you agree on a price first.
• Oysters are sold by the half dozen or dozen; restaurants also serve tagines and grilled meat for those who do not eat seafood.
• The lagoon water is calm and shallow near the beach, but the ocean side beyond the rocks has strong currents – swim only inside the lagoon.
• July and August are busy with Moroccan families; spring and autumn are quieter and still mild.

INCLUDED: private air-conditioned vehicle, driver, fuel and tolls, bottled water, pick-up and drop-off in Casablanca.
NOT INCLUDED: cistern entrance fee, lunch and drinks, boat ride, local guide in El Jadida (on request), tips.

IF THE WEATHER TURNS: the cistern is indoors and the old town is compact. On a grey or windy day lunch becomes the main event, with a warm restaurant table overlooking the lagoon, and the beach time is replaced by a short walk or an earlier return.

WHAT YOU'LL TASTE
Oualidia oysters, raw with lemon or gratinated; grilled sardines, sea bream or sole; prawns pil-pil; a seafood pastilla in some restaurants; mint tea or fresh orange juice.

PHOTO SPOTS
• The reflections and the shaft of light in the cistern (late morning is best).
• The ramparts with the ocean behind and the bastion of the Angel.
• The Porta do Mar from inside the walls.
• Colourful fishing boats on the lagoon at low tide.
• The view over the lagoon from the kasbah hill.

ACCESSIBILITY
The cistern is reached by a few steps and the floor is uneven; the old town lanes are mostly flat. The ramparts are reached by stairs. In Oualidia, restaurants and the beach are a short walk from where the car parks. Tell us about any mobility needs and we will plan the stops accordingly.

WHAT YOU TAKE AWAY: a little-known coast where Portuguese history and Moroccan seaside life meet, and the taste of oysters eaten by the lagoon where they grow.

faq.question: How long is the drive from Casablanca?
faq.answer: About 1 h 15 min to El Jadida (around 100 km on the motorway), then about 1 hour along the coast to Oualidia, and about 2 hours back to Casablanca. In total you spend around 4.5 hours in the car over a 9.5-hour day.

faq.question: Is a guide included?
faq.answer: The trip is with a private driver who knows both towns well and can show you the way around the old city. If you would like a licensed local guide for a full historical visit of El Jadida, tell us when booking and we will arrange one at an extra cost.

faq.question: What is the Portuguese Cistern?
faq.answer: An underground hall built in the early 16th century inside the Portuguese fortress of Mazagan, probably as a storeroom or armoury, and later used to hold water. Its 25 columns and brick vaults are reflected in a thin layer of water on the floor, lit by a single opening in the roof. Orson Welles filmed part of Othello here.

faq.question: Is the cistern open every day?
faq.answer: It is normally open daily with a short break at midday, but it closes from time to time for restoration. If it is closed on the day, you spend more time on the ramparts and in the old town, and we tell you in advance when we know.

faq.question: Is lunch included?
faq.answer: No, so that you can choose what and how much you eat. Your driver recommends restaurants by the lagoon. A seafood lunch usually costs about 150–300 MAD per person, depending on how many oysters and which fish you order.

faq.question: I don't eat seafood. Is there other food?
faq.answer: Yes. The lagoon restaurants also serve chicken or meat tagines, grilled meat, salads and omelettes, and vegetarian dishes can be prepared on request.

faq.question: Can I swim at Oualidia?
faq.answer: Yes. Inside the lagoon the water is calm and shallow near the beach, good for swimming and for children to paddle, especially from June to September. Do not swim on the ocean side beyond the rocks, where currents are strong.

faq.question: How much is a boat ride on the lagoon?
faq.answer: Local boatmen usually ask about 150–200 MAD for an hour per boat, not per person. You pay them directly in cash; your driver can help agree the price before you set off.

faq.question: Is the trip private?
faq.answer: Yes. The car and driver are only for your group, so you can change the timing, stay longer at the beach or skip a stop.

faq.question: Is it suitable for children?
faq.answer: Yes. Children usually love the reflections in the cistern, walking on the ramparts and playing on the calm lagoon beach. Child seats are available on request.

faq.question: When is the best time to go?
faq.answer: The trip runs all year. June to September is best for swimming but July and August are busy. Spring and autumn are quieter and pleasant. Oysters are served year-round.

faq.question: Can we add Azemmour?
faq.answer: Yes. Azemmour is on the way between Casablanca and El Jadida, and a short stop for the view of its white medina above the river adds about 20–30 minutes to the day.

faq.question: Can the trip start or end somewhere else?
faq.answer: Yes. Pick-up from Mohammed V airport or a train station is possible, and you can also be dropped off in El Jadida or continue south towards Safi or Essaouira as a one-way transfer. Ask us for the price.
